Issued at 245 PM EDT Mon Oct 12 2026

A warm, moist advective regime is underway this afternoon as a 
low level ridge axis continues to shift east of the area. The 
more impressive low level theta-e ridging is expected to develop
this evening from NE KS into SW WI just downstream of a 
progressive weak short wave trough ejecting northeast out of the
northern Rockies. Precip prospects with an initial strong 310K 
isentropic forcing surge early this evening appear to be on the 
low side as better elevated moisture profiles more capable of 
realizing some weak elevated instability will remain displaced 
to the west. By late evening and overnight, isolated showers and
thunderstorms prospects increase as upstream flattening upper 
ridge allows some steeper mid level lapse rates to advect 
eastward to the Mid MS River Valley and southern Great Lakes. 
This later timing will also coincide with the northeast 
progression of the primary low level theta-e ridge and a 
potential of some 500-750 J/kg MUCAPES. Previous forecast 
mention of slight chance PoPs north of US Route 6 still seems 
appropriate as better isentropic forcing and stronger flow on 
310K sfc remain across the north. Cannot completely discount an 
isolated shower south of US Route 6 however, given broad nature 
of advective forcing. 

In terms of temperatures, broad warm advective pattern will allow 
for unseasonably mild min temperatures tonight. Modest low level dew 
points and boundary layer decoupling should allow mins to drop into 
the mid 60s and extent of lows will depend on extent of decoupling 
and the presence of any mid level warm advection-induced 
clouds.

Pre-frontal forcing will begin to shift eastward Tuesday morning 
setting up another warm today for mid-October. The aforementioned 
western Great Lakes short wave will depart to the east, reaching the 
eastern Great Lakes by Tuesday evening. This evolution and southeast 
sinking cut-off upper Low across southwest CONUS will allow 
associated cold frontal boundary to stall across the area Tuesday 
night. Much above normal temperatures will continue Tuesday with 
some uncertainty as to extent of high temperatures. Mixing heights 
may not be particularly deep given very warm low level thermal 
profiles, but even mixing to 900 mb would support high 
temperatures in the low-mid 80s most locations (possibly upper 
80s to around 90 far south). These high temperatures would 
approach or break records for the date of October 13 (84 at FWA 
set in 1975 and 1899 and 86 at SBN set in 1975). Once again, the
extent of lingering mid level cloud will likely play a factor 
in extent of max temps.

By Tuesday night, a plume of higher level theta-e air will advect 
northward into the Mid MS Rvr Valley and eventually the southern 
Great Lakes, while another northern stream trough eventually allows 
for some frontal forcing to interact with this deeper moisture. 
Likely PoPs have been maintained late Tuesday night into early 
Wednesday afternoon with a potential of a few thunderstorms given 
likely presence of elevated instability. Frontal zone once again 
should stall and become less distinct locally later in the day 
Wednesday, setting up a lull in rain chances Wed night into early 
Thu.

Attention will then turn to a stronger short wave amplifying 
across southwest Canada, and potentially phasing with the cut-
off negative upper height anomaly across the Central Plains
towards the end of the work week. GFS deterministic may be a 
bit aggressive in phasing these features when considering bulk 
of GEFS and EC deterministic/ensemble guidance. Nonetheless, 
this northern stream wave will have some good upper level 
dynamics to work with and a stronger eastern Pacific jet to help
induce cyclogenesis across eastern Great Lakes late Thu/Fri. 

Another round of widespread rain is expected Thu/Thu evening as 
another frontal wave develops along the baroclinic zone, 
eventually drying out for Friday outside of some likely lake 
effect rain shower response. Windy conditions are also expected 
Friday, and will depend on extent of low level cyclogenesis and
low level height gradient. However, gusts into the 30 to 40 mph
range look possible during the day Friday given what should be 
fairly deep CAA-induced mixing. Some frost/freeze concerns may 
develop for Friday night/Saturday AM but will depend on 
progression of this pattern and how quickly low level 
anticyclone settles into the area and cloud cover. Greater 
chances of these frost/freeze concerns may hold off until later 
in the weekend. After a transition to below normal temps for the
weekend, temps should moderate back to, or just above normal 
levels early next week with dry weather expected Sat to Mon.
